description: Code enthusiasts that love space. (Cracked nerds 🙄)
summary:
First Light is a browser game where you design, launch and fly a crewed lunar orbiter mission, from the first sketch to the final science results.

You start in a hangar, choosing instruments, antenna, solar panels, battery, engine and fuel. A plain-language checklist shows whether the design will work. You then pick a launch vehicle and fly the mission yourself: a WASD ascent, a lunar orbit burn, a switch-flipping minigame through the day-36 eclipse, and dish re-aiming after a comms dropout. Cinematic cutscenes tie the story together.

It tackles the challenge’s trade-offs directly. Every part adds mass, draws power and costs money, so a bigger camera can mean a bigger rocket, a bigger battery and a blown budget. The game uses real physics: the rocket equation, orbital mechanics, battery and eclipse modelling, and data downlink limits. Your score covers science, cost and engineering.

The debrief links each result to real NASA data, including LRO eclipse operations, the LOLA laser altimeter and LCROSS’s discovery of water ice.

It matters because these trade-offs usually stay abstract for students. Here, anyone, even without space knowledge, learns by making choices and seeing the consequences.
details:
What it does and how it works

First Light is a browser game in which you design, launch and fly a crewed lunar orbiter. You start in a hangar and choose instruments, radio, solar panels, battery, engine and fuel. A green, yellow and red checklist tells you in plain words whether the design will work. You then pick a launch vehicle and fly the mission yourself:

  • a WASD rocket ascent;
  • a hand-flown braking burn into lunar orbit;
  • a day-36 eclipse, where you flip switches by hand to keep the battery alive;
  • dish re-aiming and instrument reboots when things break.

Cinematic cutscenes link the stages. Every part you add has a mass, a power draw and a price, so each choice pushes on the others. At the end you get a score for science, cost and engineering, plus a debrief that explains why things happened.

Benefits

It turns mission design from an abstract list of trade-offs into something you feel. If you add a bigger camera, you may need a bigger battery, a heavier ship, a bigger rocket and more money. It needs no install, runs in any modern browser on desktop or phone, and is written for people with no space background. A glossary, a "How to play" card and a step-by-step build screen guide new players.

Intended impact

We want students and the public to understand why space missions are hard, and to find that fun. After one or two runs, a player should understand why batteries, fuel margins and budgets decide missions, and want to replay it to beat the Helios benchmark score.

Tools and technology

  • HTML5, CSS3 and plain JavaScript, with Canvas 2D for the flight minigames. There are no frameworks and no server.
  • Real physics: the rocket equation, lunar gravity (real Moon constants) for the orbit burn, and a battery and eclipse model.
  • Claude (AI) helped write and test the code. Automated browser tests (Playwright) played the full game and checked the layouts.
  • AI image and video generators made the cutscenes and character art.
  • Google Fonts for type, and GitHub Pages for hosting.
  • No special hardware is needed.

NASA data

The debrief links to real NASA findings: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter eclipse operations, the LOLA laser altimeter, LCROSS's detection of water ice at Cabeus crater, and Diviner temperature measurements. Each has a source link.

Creativity

The game is a story, not a spreadsheet. It opens with the loss of the Kestrel-1 satellite in its first eclipse, and the Commander and desk heads advise you as characters. The play is hands-on, so you fly the hard moments yourself. Failure is part of the lesson.

GitHub link : https://github.com/Ormos-debug/first-light.git

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility: plain language over jargon, keyboard and on-screen controls, and skippable cutscenes.
  • Accuracy and playability: realistic physics, balanced so a careful player can reach three stars.
  • Audience: the previous winner, Zumorroda-X, showed that story-first, one-problem-at-a-time games work for non-experts.
  • Reliability: it was tested with automated playthroughs and on phone-width screens, and it handles missing media gracefully.
